results.draft_locus: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Path, Priced ¶4

results.quote: forcing brands onto one stack without measuring the benefit, or duplicating work they could share
results.finding: Declared problem_solution from 'groups that must decide what to share' to the failure pattern and the question it leaves; the one-sentence paragraph opens with no link to the VF/Zalando paragraphs before it and does not say which question the pattern leaves, so the boundary reads as a non sequitur.

results.quote: A transition is easier to see than to name.
results.finding: Declared conclusion_summary carrying over 'the signals named for each stage in turn'; the opening never refers back to the per-stage ending signals it gathers, so the move from the Group decision table to a cross-stage signals table is unexplained (flow reader A found this section's position unclear).

results.draft_locus: Stage by Stage ¶10; When It Goes Wrong ¶2
results.quote: The temptation at this stage is
results.finding: The Giant's Boots is presented as the Omnichannel stage's temptation, but the failure-pattern box and 'Too early' attach it to a Growing-stage merchant; the reader cannot tell which stage it belongs to. The prose never says it means copying a later stage's architecture at whatever stage one is in.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 5 (The Giant's Boots defined for Growing, called the Omnichannel temptation, then Growing again)

results.quote: For a 14-person team the honest reading is
results.finding: The 14-person team appears with no antecedent; the chapter never says it is Kestrel & Pine's team (the map says 10–20), so the reader must infer whose team is meant.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 6 (nothing says Kestrel & Pine has 14 engineers)

results.quote: forcing brands onto one stack without measuring the benefit, or duplicating work they could share
results.finding: The one-sentence One Size Fits None paragraph sits between the Zalando acquisition paragraph and the Zalando/Uber autonomy cautions with no connection to either, splitting the run of group evidence; the prose does not show that the next paragraph is evidence for the pattern's second half (too much autonomy).
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 7 (the one-line paragraph splits the Zalando material and stops the flow)

results.quote: The EDI request often comes first because
results.finding: The claim that the EDI request comes first is placed at the end of the paragraph, after five other signals have been listed, so 'first' contradicts where it sits and reads as a step back; the Eurostat support belongs beside the EDI signal.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 8 (the 'first' statistic at the end of the list seemed to contradict its position)

results.quote: Its shape had changed in 2023, but the signals went unread until the April 2027 stage map named the change.
results.finding: Six signals counted in 2026 for a shape change in 2023 reads as contradicting the two-signal rule and the key point that signals arrive before the change; the prose does not say that signals were already present in 2023 (Duiven, the enterprise tier, per the table) and went on accumulating unread.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 9 (2026 signals for a 2023 change clash with 'signals arrive before'; unclear whether signals predict or confirm)

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Stage Map ¶3
results.finding: 'Therefore' makes Waypoint's scope follow from the stage map and from the absence of Group signals, although the previous paragraph says Waypoint launched in March 2027, before the April map, and the real reason (the Growing-stage leftovers) comes only in the next paragraph; readers re-read to sort out cause and timeline.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 item 1 (Waypoint launched a month before the map, yet 'therefore' implies the map produced it)

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Stage Map ¶4
results.quote: That row is this chapter's argument.
results.finding: The paragraph speaks of 'one entry on the map' and 'that row' before the reader has seen any map with rows, so it is unclear which row is meant.

results.quote: A transition is easier to see than to name.
results.finding: Flow reader A found the signals section's place after the Group decision table unclear: the reader goes from Group to a cross-stage table and back to the case, and the opening does not say that the table gathers the ending signals each stage section named.
The count of six 2026 signals includes a standing condition (three definitions of 'order') rather than an event of that year, so the count reads as padded.

results.quote: open-source platforms stop being free above Shopware's €1 million GMV line
results.finding: Repeats the vendor-tier evidence already given in the definition section without saying it is a recall, so the reader thinks it has been read before.

results.draft_locus: The Map: Four Stages Side by Side table
results.finding: 'Interchange-plus pricing' is used in the map's fees row and never explained; it is not among the glosses the audience already has.
results.corroborated_by: flow-B, section 3 last item (interchange-plus pricing in the map is not explained)

results.quote: tenancy (one tenant per brand or a tenant of tenants)
results.finding: 'Tenant'/'tenancy' is used from the callout and the map onward and is only illustrated, never defined; not on already_knows.

A new, unexplained label ('fair-use line') for what the definition section called a paid plan required above €1 million GMV; the inconsistency leaves the reader unsure whether these are the same threshold.

results.draft_locus: The Map: Four Stages Side by Side table
results.finding: 'Per-entity books' and 'intercompany flows' in the Group column are never explained for a newcomer reader.
